questions.stem: Why do two sets of intercostal muscles exist?

options.text: Muscles can only pull, so opposite sets take turns moving the ribs each way
options.explanation: Antagonistic pairing solves the push problem.
Speed comes from contraction strength, not muscle count.
Surface count is irrelevant.
Both sets work, in alternation.

questions.stem: Which muscles contract during normal inhalation?

options.explanation: Abdominals play no named role here.

options.text: The external intercostals and the diaphragm
options.explanation: Ribs rise and the diaphragm flattens together.
The internal set works in forced exhalation.
The external set works alongside it.

questions.stem: What shape does the diaphragm take when relaxed?

options.explanation: It domes upwards, not downwards.
No twisting occurs.

options.text: Domed, curving upwards into the chest
options.explanation: Relaxation lets it spring back to its dome.
Flat is the contracted shape.

questions.stem: What does antagonistic mean for these muscles?

options.explanation: That would fight itself.

options.text: They share the same nerve supply
options.explanation: Nerve sharing is not the term's point.

options.text: They pull in the same direction
options.explanation: Opposite directions are the essence.

options.text: While one contracts, the other relaxes, giving opposite movements
options.explanation: The pairing produces motion in both directions.

questions.stem: Which movement do the internal intercostals drive?

options.text: Pulling the ribs down and in during forced exhalation
options.explanation: That is the internal set's job.
That is the external set's job.
The diaphragm moves itself.
Stillness is not their role.

questions.stem: Name the two sets of intercostal muscles.
questions.modelAnswer: The external intercostal muscles and the internal intercostal muscles.

questions.stem: State the diaphragm's two shapes during breathing.
questions.modelAnswer: Contracted and flattened during inhalation; relaxed and domed during exhalation.

questions.stem: Explain why the rib cage cannot be pushed down directly to exhale.
questions.modelAnswer: Because muscles only pull on bones, never push; lowering the ribs therefore needs a second set of muscles — the internal intercostals — pulling from the opposite geometry, which is exactly why the antagonistic arrangement exists.

questions.stem: Blowing out birthday candles demands more than a relaxed exhale. Name the muscles at work and their actions.
questions.modelAnswer: The internal intercostals contract to pull the ribs down and in, shrinking the thorax further than relaxation alone; the diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards; together they force air out hard enough to reach the candles.

questions.stem: What happens to thorax volume during inhalation?

options.explanation: The change is real but not a fixed doubling.
Raised ribs and a flattened diaphragm enlarge the cavity.
That is exhalation.
Volume change is the whole mechanism.

questions.stem: Why does air enter the lungs during inhalation?

options.text: Because the ribs create a vacuum
options.explanation: No vacuum forms; just a lower pressure.

options.text: Because the diaphragm pushes air in
options.explanation: The diaphragm's flattening enlarges the space; it does not push air.

options.text: Because pressure inside falls below atmospheric, so air flows in
options.explanation: Air moves down its pressure gradient.

options.text: Because the lungs suck air by muscle power directly
options.explanation: Muscles change volume; the pressure difference does the pulling.

options.text: Diaphragm contracts, ribs rise, air enters
options.explanation: That is inhalation.

options.text: Ribs rise, volume rises, pressure falls
options.explanation: Those are inhalation events.

options.text: Volume falls, pressure falls, air enters
options.explanation: Falling volume raises pressure.

options.text: Diaphragm relaxes and domes, ribs drop, volume falls, pressure rises, air leaves
options.explanation: That is the full reversal of inhalation.

questions.stem: When would forced exhalation be used?

options.text: During strenuous activity, to clear carbon dioxide faster
options.explanation: Hard exercise demands quicker waste clearance.
Sleeping uses quiet breathing.
Sneezing is one case, not the general one.
It is routine during exercise.

questions.stem: What does the term ventilation mean?

options.explanation: Filtering is a defensive extra, not ventilation.

options.text: The movement of air into and out of the lungs
options.explanation: Breathing in and out is the whole definition.

options.text: The exchange of gases in the alveoli
options.explanation: Gas exchange happens after ventilation delivers the air.
That is cardiac, not respiratory.

questions.stem: List the four events of inhalation in order.
questions.modelAnswer: Diaphragm contracts and flattens, external intercostals raise the ribs, thorax volume increases, and air is drawn in as pressure falls.

questions.stem: Which pressure relationship drives airflow in both directions?
questions.modelAnswer: Air flows from higher pressure to lower pressure, whether entering or leaving.

questions.stem: Explain why learning inhalation thoroughly prepares you for exhalation questions.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the two sequences are near-exact opposites — every contraction becomes a relaxation, every volume rise becomes a fall, every pressure drop becomes a rise — so mastering one direction hands you the other for free.

questions.stem: A runner finishes a sprint breathing hard and fast. Explain the forced exhalation benefit in terms of gas exchange.
questions.modelAnswer: The sprint loaded her blood with carbon dioxide from the working muscles; forced exhalation shrinks the thorax further than relaxed breathing would, pushing air out faster and clearing that carbon dioxide at the rate the exercise produced it.
